title: QuantumForge throughput & routing discovery
summary: Initial latency/throughput discovery for a real-time assistant product. Customer served use case, p95 latency goals, concurrency profile, and where Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private fit. Agreed to run token/sec benchmarks and a small canary on Dedicated; Redwood to send perf spreadsheet and share routing/caching notes.
transcript:
Header: 2026-02-20 16:00 UTC | Duration 48m | Recording: automatic
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Ethan Rivera (CTO - QuantumForge), Priya Singh (ML Eng), Liam O'Neal (SRE)

00:00:04 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, I'm Maya from Redwood, joining with Jordan on the deep infra side. Quick agenda, we'll walk p95 goals, concurrency, streaming behaviour, then map to Hosted/Dedicated/Private options.
00:00:20 Ethan: Yep, thanks. We wanted to confirm numbers before we start internal infra work, so really appreciate it.
00:00:28 Jordan: Cool, and quick clarify — is this for the live chat assistant only or also batch summarization?
00:00:33 Priya: Primarily live assistant (low-latency), some background batch embed jobs but main headache is the assistant. Target 95th percentile across user-facing requests.
00:00:45 Mia (transcription error for Maya): uh Maya: we got it, thanks.
00:00:50 Ethan: Our SLA target for product is p95 < 300ms for the user-facing streaming tokens. We know that's aggressive but our UX team has measured drop-off at anything above ~350.
00:01:05 Jordan: Understood. Couple quick follow-ups — what does a typical request look like? Sequence length, prompt plus history?
00:01:12 Priya: Average input tokens 120, reply tokens variable 40-350, but 95th reply tokens ~280. We do streaming so latency to first token matters a lot and then sustained token/sec for the stream.
00:01:27 Liam: We also have spikes during product launches — we see concurrent active sessions jump from 200 to ~1,200 for 4-6 minutes.
00:01:38 Jordan: That's helpful. So two axes: steady-state concurrency ~200-ish, burst concurrency up to 1.2k for short windows. Workload is mostly many small streams not giant single long chats.
00:01:50 Maya: High-level mapping: Hosted is simplest to stand up and we can meet moderate p95 goals for smaller models; Dedicated gives predictable capacity and faster cold-starts on KV cache; Private if you need VPC/air-gap. But specifics depend on model size, quantization, and batching.
00:02:08 Ethan: Question — can Hosted meet the 300ms p95 for 280-token responses when streaming?
00:02:15 Jordan: The p95 number is largely dominated by first-token time and initial KV/cache warm state. For large models (13B+), Hosted can meet sub-300ms first-token sometimes with the right serving stack and streaming, but it's not guaranteed at high concurrency without Dedicated capacity or caching. Our suggestions: prefix caching for repeated system prompts, model choice (smaller distilled models or 7B variants), and aggressive batching rules for cost.
00:02:36 Priya: We plan to use a 13B model—quality requirements stop us from going smaller. Are there quantized variants you recommend?
00:02:44 Jordan: Yes, 4-bit quantization + optimized kernels help throughput significantly (and reduce GPU memory), but you get some quality drift; we can recommend tuned quant profiles and run evals.
00:02:55 Ethan: For benchmarking, we need token/sec numbers. At 200 steady concurrency with 250-token average response, what should we expect?
00:03:05 Jordan: Ballpark — on a single dedicated A100-style instance with optimized kernels and batching, you're looking at X tokens/sec per-GPU depending on model. (transcription note: Jordan says "X" while sketching numbers, later will send spreadsheet). For planning, assume ~300-500 tokens/sec per-GPU for 13B quant on our optimized runtime under ideal batching. But streaming reduces batching efficiency so effective tokens/sec drops.
00:03:28 Priya: So we'd need what, 3-5 GPUs to handle 200 concurrent steady sessions?
00:03:34 Jordan: Rough estimate: if each concurrent stream consumes ~2-3 tokens/sec on average while streaming it's more about throughput to sustain all streams — rough calc: 200 sessions * 2 tokens/sec = 400 tokens/sec sustained, so a single optimized GPU could cover this, but headroom for bursts and latency SLOs recommends multiple GPUs and autoscaling. For p95 latency targets during spikes you'd want Dedicated pool sized to absorb the 1.2k peak or route excess to lower-cost tier.
00:03:57 Maya: Important: Redwood routing policies let you send traffic to Hosted for normal and failover to Dedicated or lower-cost variants if Dedicated saturated. We can set a region/cost/latency routing rule.
00:04:09 Ethan: How about cold KV cache — in a burst where many users have different prefixes, how long does warmup typically take?
00:04:18 Jordan: If prefixes are unique, warmup means generating KV entries again — that's request path work. We bake in incremental warming: you can pre-warm common prefixes, and we suggest a small warm pool. Cold-start to first token might be 80-200ms extra depending on model; once KV warmed, subsequent tokens are faster. Note: transcription sometimes renders KV as "K V cash" or "K V cache".
00:04:38 Priya: Streaming specifics — we need first-token under 150ms ideally, then sustain 15-25 tokens/sec. Is that realistic?
00:04:48 Jordan: First-token <150ms is tough at scale for 13B unless you use Dedicated and pinned model instances with KV cache warm and no cold migrations. 150-300ms is more typical for first-token on hosted with warm cache. Sustained 15-25 tokens/sec is high per-session; more common is 3-5 tokens/sec per session unless you configure model and chunking to be aggressive. If you chunk tokens aggressively (shorter output chunks), you can increase tokens/sec but risk more overhead and quality/regression.
00:05:14 Ethan: Hmm, our UX wants needle-like snappiness. Let's talk numbers for canary: what if we run a dedicated canary with 4 GPUs for a week?
00:05:23 Maya: That's sensible. For a canary Redwood recommends: mirror a slice of traffic, 4 GPUs with pinned 13B quant instances, pre-load KV cache for top 10% prefixes, and run token/sec traces. We'll provide a perf workbook with expected p50/p95/p99 and token/sec benchmarks.
00:05:38 Liam: Instrumentation — what traces do you provide? We need token-level timing and per-request cost breakdowns.
00:05:45 Jordan: Console provides token timing, per-route latency, cost breakdowns, and traces. We also give exportable CSVs for offline analysis.
00:05:52 Priya: Any notes about fallback behavior — if Dedicated overloaded do you failover to hosted or queue? We can't drop sessions.
00:05:59 Maya: We support automatic fallback to Hosted or to a lower-capacity model variant, plus queuing policies. You can configure fail-open vs fail-closed. We recommend failover to a slightly smaller model for short bursts to keep sessions alive while you auto-scale Dedicated.
00:06:12 Ethan: Competitor question — are there customers running similar profiles on OpenAI or Anthropic and how do those compare for p95?
00:06:20 Jordan: Many customers start on public APIs; they often see unpredictable p95 under heavy concurrency and lack of control for caching/batching. Redwood's Dedicated gives more predictability and routing control. (slight crosstalk) Also we integrate with private deployments if strict data residency needed.
00:06:34 Priya: Ok next steps — we'll want the perf workbook and a short test plan we can run against our staging.
00:06:42 Maya: Great, we'll send that. Also list of security docs — SOC2, iso, and network designs for Private if you need.
00:06:49 Ethan: Timeline — we want a pilot in 3 weeks. Is that feasible?
00:06:53 Maya: Yes, pilot feasible in 2-4 weeks depending on provisioning and sample size.
00:06:58 Jordan: I'll also propose a simple benchmark harness: scripted streaming requests with realistic token distributions and a sidecar that records first-token latency and sustained token/sec per session.
00:07:10 Priya: Sounds good. A quick clarifier — what's the expected p95 improvement if we go Dedicated vs Hosted for a 13B quant?
00:07:18 Jordan: Hard to promise exact numbers without run, but many customers see 20-40% p95 reduction on first-token and much smaller variance. Dedicated reduces jitter and cold-start spikes; caching strategy determines steady-state.
00:07:30 Ethan: Anything about price? We need a rough cost projection for 4 GPU canary and steady Dedicated pool to show to finance.
00:07:37 Maya: We'll include model/GPU cost breakdowns in the workbook, plus routing/cost tradeoffs— e.g., keep 2 reserved GPUs for steady-state and autoscale up to N for bursts; cost delta between hosted per-token and dedicated reserved capacity will be shown.
00:07:51 Liam: For observability, can we tag traces by customer feature flag?
00:07:55 Jordan: Yes, you can attach metadata, route tags, and token-level identifiers for debugging.
00:08:02 Ethan: Recap then: Redwood to send perf workbook, short runbook for canary, security docs, and propose pilot start date. We'll attempt to mirror 10% of traffic to the canary and collect p95 first-token and sustained tokens/sec.
00:08:18 Maya: Correct. Anything else?
00:08:22 Priya: One small ask — can you include a note about quantization regression checks in the workbook? We need model-quality baselines.
00:08:30 Jordan: Absolutely, we'll include evaluation prompts and metrics to compare.
00:08:35 Maya: Ok thanks all, we'll follow up with next steps in email.
00:08:39 Ethan: Thanks everyone.

(Transcript fidelity: medium — occasional word swaps and punctuation issues)
